title: AP Reported Trump Ordered Iran Strikes During Air Force One Flight After Consulting Republican Lawmakers
description_medium: An Associated Press timeline says President Donald Trump ordered Operation Epic Fury at 3:38 p.m. Eastern on Feb. 27, 2026, while flying to Texas. During the flight, he asked Republican lawmakers whether to continue negotiations with Iran or strike; an unnamed person familiar with the conversation said those present generally viewed talks as a delay tactic. Trump did not tell the lawmakers what he planned to do, according to AP.
description_long: The Associated Press timeline of the Iran strike decision reports that Trump asked a small group of Republican lawmakers aboard Air Force One for their views on whether to continue negotiations or attack. The discussion took place during the flight to Texas on Feb. 27, 2026, after Trump had told reporters at 12:25 p.m. that he was unhappy with nuclear talks and had not made a final decision. He issued the order for Operation Epic Fury at 3:38 p.m. A person with direct knowledge, speaking anonymously, said the lawmakers discussed the merits of negotiations and a strike and that the general sentiment was that Iran was using talks as a delay tactic. Among those aboard were Texas Sens. John Cornyn and Ted Cruz. AP later reported that Cornyn said Trump had not told them what he would do. The operation began at 1:15 a.m. Eastern the next day, according to Joint Chiefs Chair Gen. Dan Caine’s timeline. The report provides a concrete account of limited consultation and its timing, but does not establish that lawmakers’ views determined the decision or that dissent was suppressed.

title: Guardian Feature Collected Seven Episodes From Trump’s First Year Back in Office
description_medium: A Guardian feature published Jan. 23, 2026, collected seven episodes it described as perplexing. It reported that Trump appeared to fall asleep during meetings, told an inaccurate story about his uncle teaching Ted Kaczynski, made unsupported claims about wind turbines and whales, and confused Greenland with Iceland at Davos. The roundup did not report that later claims were assessed against it.
description_long: The Guardian’s Jan. 23, 2026 feature brought together seven episodes from Donald Trump’s first year back in office. Its examples included his apparent dozing during government meetings, a story connecting his uncle to Ted Kaczynski that the article said could not be true, and unprompted claims that wind turbines make whales “loco.” It also covered Trump’s confusion of Greenland with Iceland in a Davos speech and press secretary Karoline Leavitt’s social-media denial that he had mixed them up. The article quoted White House representatives describing Trump as energetic and mentally sharp, while noting that psychiatrists and political opponents had raised concerns about his conduct. It was an editorial roundup of public moments and reactions, not a clinical evaluation. The piece does not document use of the article as a credibility benchmark for later statements or measure public trust. Its concrete contribution is the contemporaneous collection of examples and the contrasting official responses.

title: NPR Found 53 Pages of Epstein-Related FBI Records Appeared Missing From Public Database
description_medium: An NPR investigation compared file serial numbers in DOJ’s public Epstein database with FBI records and Maxwell-case discovery logs. NPR found that 53 pages of interview reports and notes appeared to be missing, including records tied to a woman who alleged that Trump abused her when she was a minor. The allegation was unverified; DOJ declined to explain the specific pages, and the White House denied wrongdoing by Trump.
description_long: NPR’s Feb. 24, 2026 investigation examined document serial numbers and logs related to records from the Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell investigations. It found that 53 pages of FBI interview reports and notes appeared to be missing from the Justice Department’s public database. The records included materials associated with a woman who alleged that Donald Trump abused her when she was a minor. NPR reported that only the first of four FBI interviews was public and that it did not mention Trump. The accusation remains unverified; the reporting does not establish wrongdoing by Trump. DOJ declined to answer questions about the specific records and why they were not available. The White House said Trump had been exonerated regarding Epstein and denied wrongdoing. NPR separately reported that records involving another woman, a witness in Maxwell’s prosecution, had been removed and that some were later restored. The investigation described gaps in the public record and competing statements about the release process. It did not measure a political effect or show that Trump directed the handling of the files.

description_long: NPR’s investigation compared the public database of Epstein records with serial-number sequences in FBI case files, emails and discovery documents turned over to Ghislaine Maxwell’s attorneys. The review indicated that 53 pages of interview reports and notes were not publicly available. For a woman who alleged that Trump abused her when she was a minor, NPR found records showing four FBI interviews, but only the first interview appeared in the public database; that document did not mention Trump. The White House denied wrongdoing by Trump. These particulars describe what NPR’s cross-check found and the different explanations offered for records’ absence. title: Guardian Reported Three FBI Interview Memos Missing From DOJ’s Initial Epstein-Records Release
description_medium: The Guardian reported that DOJ’s first large Epstein-records release omitted three FBI memos covering four interviews from 2019. An administration official confirmed the reports were authentic, while DOJ told NPR that withheld records were duplicative or privileged. The memos contained an unsubstantiated allegation about Trump; no charges followed, and Trump denies wrongdoing.
description_long: The Guardian’s Feb. 26, 2026 report said three FBI Form 302 memos documenting four interviews from 2019 were not included in the Justice Department’s initial upload of millions of Epstein-related pages. The newspaper obtained the memos and reported that an administration official confirmed they were authentic. Only the first interview, in which the woman did not name Trump, had appeared in the public release. The reports contained an allegation involving Donald Trump and Jeffrey Epstein; the Guardian described it as unsubstantiated, said it contradicted known information about Epstein in the early 1980s, and reported that the FBI never brought charges related to it. Trump has denied wrongdoing. DOJ told NPR that nothing had been deleted and that withheld material was duplicative or privileged. These statements leave a disagreement over disclosure status and the reason records were not initially published. The reporting does not show that Trump controlled the decision or that the allegation was established.

title: AP Reported 16 Epstein-Related Files Disappeared From DOJ Webpage on Dec. 20, 2025
description_medium: The Associated Press reported that at least 16 files disappeared from DOJ’s Epstein-records webpage less than a day after they were posted. The missing items included nude-painting images and a photograph of Donald Trump with Jeffrey Epstein, Melania Trump and Ghislaine Maxwell inside a larger image of a drawer. DOJ had not explained the removal at publication; the photo was restored after review the next day.
description_long: The Associated Press reported on Dec. 20, 2025, that at least 16 files were no longer accessible on the Justice Department’s public webpage for Epstein-related records, less than a day after they had been posted. The missing set included images of paintings depicting nude women and a photograph showing Donald Trump with Jeffrey Epstein, Melania Trump and Ghislaine Maxwell inside a drawer in a larger picture of a credenza. DOJ had not said whether the removal was intentional or why the files were unavailable when AP published its report. On Dec. 21, the department restored the photograph after reviewing it and saying no victim appeared in the image. Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche said the file had been temporarily removed after victim-advocacy concerns, not to protect Trump. The initial article also described wider criticism of the first release, including heavy redactions, omitted records and a rolling-release schedule that missed the date set by Congress. Those broader disclosure issues provide context for why the brief disappearance drew attention, without proving a motive for the removal.
